A tile path in a park features three congruent equilateral tiles arranged in a straight line. One of the tiles is shaded. If the total perimeter of the tile arrangement is [MATH: 20] centimeters, what is the area of the shaded region, in square centimeters?

sections.normalized_html:
The perimeter of the row formed by the three congruent equilateral triangles consists of five outer triangle sides. If [MATH: s] is the side length of each small triangle, then: [MATH: Perimeter|= 20; 5s|= 20; s|= (20)/(5); = 4]

Now, we calculate the area of the shaded equilateral triangle using the formula: [MATH: A|= (sqrt(3))/(4)s^{2}; = (sqrt(3))/(4) ⋅ 4^{2}; = (sqrt(3))/(4) ⋅ 16; = 4sqrt(3)]

Therefore, the area of the shaded region is [MATH: 4\sqrt{3}] square centimeters.

sections.normalized_html:
In an equilateral triangle, all three sides are equal. So if the perimeter is [MATH: 432,] then each side has length [MATH: \dfrac{432}{3} = 144.]

To find the height of an equilateral triangle, we draw an altitude from one vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. This altitude splits the equilateral triangle into two [MATH: 30^\circ]–[MATH: 60^\circ]–[MATH: 90^\circ] right triangles.

In a [MATH: 30^\circ]–[MATH: 60^\circ]–[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle:

  • The hypotenuse is the side of the equilateral triangle, which is [MATH: 144.]

  • The shorter leg is half the base: [MATH: \dfrac{144}{2} = 72.]

  • The height is the longer leg, which is [MATH: \sqrt{3}] times the shorter leg.

So, the height is [MATH: 72\sqrt{3}.]

Thus, the value of [MATH: k] is [MATH: 72.]

sections.normalized_html:
For a [MATH: 30^\circ]–[MATH: 60^\circ]–[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle, we have the following:

  • The shorter leg is opposite the [MATH: 30^\circ] angle.

  • The longer leg is opposite the [MATH: 60^\circ] angle.

  • The hypotenuse is twice the length of the shorter leg.

  • The longer leg is [MATH: \sqrt{3}] times the length of the shorter leg.

Let the shortest side have length [MATH: x.] Then the perimeter is [MATH: x + x\sqrt{3} + 2x = 3x + x\sqrt{3}.]

We are told that the perimeter is [MATH: 15 + 5\sqrt{3},] so we write [MATH: 3x + x\sqrt{3} = 15 + 5\sqrt{3}.]

Next, we group terms on the left and solve for [MATH: x{:}] [MATH: x(3 + sqrt(3))|= 15 + 5sqrt(3); x|= (15 + 5sqrt(3))/(3 + sqrt(3)); = (5(3 + sqrt(3)))/(3 + sqrt(3)); = 5]

So, the shortest side is [MATH: 5,] and the longest side, the hypotenuse, is [MATH: 2x = 2(5) = 10.]
